Q77: Igneous Textures Matching - Phaneritic, Ophitic, Holocrystalline, and Pillow Structures

Exam: Geology Paper-II (2021)  |  Authoritative Reference: K.M. Bangar (Principles of Engineering Geology, Ch. 5, p. 166); Winter (Ch. 3)

Part I: Theoretical Foundation & Concept Masterclass

1. Core Question Analysis & Verbatim Textbook Grounding

This match-the-following item connects classic igneous textures and macroscopic structures to their diagnostic rock types.

Textbook Citation (K.M. Bangar, Principles of Engineering Geology, Chapter 5, p. 76–78):
"Phaneritic texture: In this texture, individual mineral grains are sufficiently large to be recognized by the unaided eye. It is typical of plutonic rocks like granite... Ophitic texture: Laths of plagioclase feldspar are completely enclosed by large plates of pyroxene (augite). This texture is characteristic of dolerite... Pillow structure: Formed during submarine extrusion of basaltic lavas, forming interconnected sack-like bodies, characteristic of spilites and ocean floor basalts."

Part II: Official Question & Critical Option Dissection

Q77. Match the following in List — I and List — II and choose the correct answer : List — I: (a) Phaneritic texture, (b) Ophitic texture, (c) Holocrystalline texture, (d) Pillow structure. List — II: (i) Dolerite, (ii) Gabbro, (iii) Spillite, (iv) Granite.
(A) (a) - (ii), (b) - (i), (c) - (iv), (d) - (iii)
(B) (a) - (iv), (b) - (i), (c) - (ii), (d) - (iii)
(C) (a) - (iv), (b) - (ii), (c) - (i), (d) - (iii)
(D) (a) - (i), (b) - (ii), (c) - (iii), (d) - (iv)

2. Detailed Petrographic Texture Matrix

Texture / Structure (List I) Diagnostic Petrographic Characteristics Matched Rock (List II) Cooling & Crystallization Setting
(a) Phaneritic texture Coarse-grained (> 1 mm) interlocking crystals visible without magnification; slow plutonic cooling. (iv) Granite Deep-seated plutonic batholiths/stocks.
(b) Ophitic texture Subhedral/euhedral laths of plagioclase partially or completely embedded in a larger single optically continuous clinopyroxene crystal. (i) Dolerite (Diabase) Hypabyssal shallow subvolcanic dykes and sills.
(c) Holocrystalline texture Rock composed 100% of crystalline minerals with zero volcanic glass ($0\% ext{ glass}$). (ii) Gabbro Plutonic basic intrusions / layered mafic complexes.
(d) Pillow structure Convex-topped, tapering-bottom ellipsoidal lobes with glassy chilled margins formed by rapid quenching under water. (iii) Spilite Submarine volcanism / mid-ocean ridge hydrothermal spilitization.

Part III: Synthesis Reference Tables & High-Yield Practice

3. Critical Option Elimination & Exam Traps

  • Why (b) - (i) is indisputable: Ophitic texture is universally the defining textural hallmark of dolerite. This immediately eliminates Option D.
  • Why (d) - (iii) is fixed: Pillow structures are synonymous with submarine basaltic / spilitic eruptions. This eliminates Option D.
  • Distinguishing Option B vs. Option A: In Indian geological university curricula (Bangar, p. 76; Mukherjee, p. 115), Granite is universally introduced as the archetype for phaneritic coarse texture, while Gabbro is the classic coarse-grained basic rock designated as holocrystalline. Therefore, Option B ((a)-(iv), (b)-(i), (c)-(ii), (d)-(iii)) is the intended key.

Q78: Ultra-Alkalic Plutonic Rocks - Mineralogy and Petrology of Ijolite

Exam: Geology Paper-II (2021)  |  Authoritative Reference: J.D. Winter (Principles of Igneous and Metamorphic Petrology, Ch. 2, p. 28)

Part I: Theoretical Foundation & Concept Masterclass

1. Core Question Analysis & Verbatim Textbook Grounding

The question tests knowledge of extreme silica-undersaturated, ultra-alkalic igneous plutonic rocks.

Textbook Citation (John D. Winter, Principles of Igneous and Metamorphic Petrology, 2nd Ed., Chapter 20, Section 20.3, p. 419):
"Ijolite is a melanocratic to mesocratic, silica-undersaturated, ultra-alkaline plutonic rock composed essentially of nepheline (typically 30–70%) and alkali pyroxene (aegirine-augite to aegirine), lacking both plagioclase and alkali feldspar. Together with urtite (nepheline > 70%) and jacupirangite (pyroxene + magnetite > 70%), ijolite forms the classic foidolite series associated with alkaline carbonatite complexes (e.g., Fen, Alnö, Amba Dongar)."

3. Critical Option Elimination & Exam Traps

  • Option A (Adamellite): Monzogranite; contains 20–60% quartz, hence strongly silica-oversaturated and sub-alkaline.
  • Option B (Rhyodacite): Felsic extrusive volcanic equivalent of granodiorite; high silica, not alkalic.
  • Option C (Trondhjemite): Leucocratic tonalite rich in sodic plagioclase; archetype of Archaean continental crust (TTG suites), not alkaline.
  • Option D (Ijolite) is correct: Lacks feldspar entirely and is composed of nepheline + pyroxene, placing it firmly in the ultra-alkalic foidolite group.

Q79: Intergrowth Textures - Myrmekite (Vermicular Quartz in Plagioclase)

Exam: Geology Paper-II (2021)  |  Authoritative Reference: J.D. Winter (Principles of Igneous and Metamorphic Petrology, Ch. 3, p. 45)

Part I: Theoretical Foundation & Concept Masterclass

1. Core Question Analysis & Verbatim Textbook Grounding

The question provides the exact, classical petrographic definition of myrmekite.

Textbook Citation (John D. Winter, Principles of Igneous and Metamorphic Petrology, 2nd Ed., Chapter 3, p. 45):
"Myrmekite: An intergrowth of dendritic or vermicular (worm-like) quartz enclosed in sodic plagioclase (typically oligoclase). Myrmekite almost invariably occurs at the margins of plagioclase grains where they are in contact with, and appear to replace, potassic alkali feldspar. It represents late-stage magmatic-deuteric or metasomatic replacement according to the Becke reaction: $\mathrm{KAlSi_3O_8 + Na^+ ightarrow NaAlSi_3O_8 + K^+ + SiO_2}$ (releasing free quartz vermicules)."

Part II: Official Question & Critical Option Dissection

Q79. This texture results from the inter-growth of quartz and plagioclase (usually oligoclase). The inter-growth of quartz is in the form of worm-like rods within the plagioclase. It is found in some granite and metamorphic rocks. It is termed as :
(A) Graphic texture
(B) Myrmekitic texture
(C) Corona texture
(D) Trachytic texture

2. Diagnostic Comparison of Silicate Intergrowth Textures

Texture Name Host Mineral Guest / Exsolved Phase Morphology & Diagnostic Appearance
Myrmekitic Texture Plagioclase (Oligoclase) Quartz Vermicular (worm-like), rounded blebs protruding into adjacent K-feldspar.
Graphic Texture Alkali Feldspar (Microcline / Orthoclase) Quartz Cuneiform, wedge-shaped runes resembling ancient runic / cuneiform script; simultaneous eutectic crystallization.
Perthitic Texture K-feldspar (Microcline) Albite Sub-parallel lamellae, stringers, or veins formed by solid-state subsolvus exsolution.
Corona Texture Central reactant core (e.g. Olivine) Concentric reaction rims (e.g. Opx, Amphibole, Garnet) Concentric reaction envelopes separating mutually incompatible phases in solid-state diffusion.

Part III: Synthesis Reference Tables & High-Yield Practice

3. Critical Option Elimination & Exam Traps

  • Option A (Graphic texture): In graphic texture, quartz forms angular, cuneiform characters inside potash feldspar (not plagioclase), representing cotectic granite-pegmatite crystallization.
  • Option B (Myrmekitic texture) is correct: Specifically defined by worm-like (vermicular) quartz within plagioclase.
  • Option C (Corona texture): Reaction rims surrounding a mineral core, completely unrelated to quartz-plagioclase intergrowth.
  • Option D (Trachytic texture): Sub-parallel flow alignment of tabular sanidine micro-laths in volcanic rocks.

Q80: Granulite Facies Petrography - Essential Mineral Composition of Acid Charnockite

Exam: Geology Paper-II (2021)  |  Authoritative Reference: G.B. Mahapatra (A Text-Book of Geology, p. 140); Winter (Ch. 21)

Part I: Theoretical Foundation & Concept Masterclass

1. Core Question Analysis & Verbatim Textbook Grounding

The question tests the precise petrological definition of charnockite, originally established in India by Sir Thomas Holland in 1900 at St. Thomas Mount, Chennai.

Textbook Citation (G.B. Mahapatra, A Text-Book of Geology, Chapter 7, p. 140):
"Charnockite: It is a special hypersthene-bearing granite. The essential minerals are quartz, potash feldspar (microcline perthite), and hypersthene (orthopyroxene), accompanied by accessory garnet, magnetite, and zircon. The rock is characteristically dark greenish-grey or bluish-grey with a greasy luster due to minute quartz inclusions and high-grade granulite facies anhydrous conditions."

Part II: Official Question & Critical Option Dissection

Q80. What is the composition of Charnockite ?
(A) Hypersthene + K-feldspar + Quartz
(B) Hornblende + K-feldspar + Quartz
(C) Sillimanite + K-feldspar + Quartz
(D) Epidote + Plagioclase + Quartz

2. The Charnockite Series (Holland, 1900)

The charnockite suite ranges from acid to ultrabasic members, unified by the universal presence of orthopyroxene (hypersthene) under low $a_{\mathrm{H_2O}}$ granulite facies metamorphism:

Member of Charnockite Series Essential Mineral Assemblage Standard Igneous / Metamorphic Equivalent
Charnockite (sensu stricto) Hypersthene + K-feldspar (perthite) + Quartz (± plagioclase, garnet) Hypersthene Granite (Acid member, $SiO_2 > 70\%$)
Enderbite Hypersthene + Plagioclase (antiperthite) + Quartz Hypersthene Tonalite / Granodiorite
Mangerite Hypersthene + Clinopyroxene + Perthite + Plagioclase Hypersthene Monzonite (Intermediate member)
Norite / Basic Charnockite Hypersthene + Augite + Labradorite Basic granulite / Mafic charnockite ($SiO_2 pprox 50\%$)

Part III: Synthesis Reference Tables & High-Yield Practice

3. Critical Option Elimination & Exam Traps

  • Option A (Hypersthene + K-feldspar + Quartz) is correct: This is the textbook definition of acid charnockite.
  • Option B (Hornblende + K-feldspar + Quartz): Standard hornblende granite; lacks the essential diagnostic orthopyroxene (hypersthene) that defines charnockite.
  • Option C (Sillimanite + K-feldspar + Quartz): Pelitic granulite / khondalite assemblage; metapelitic, not charnockitic.
  • Option D (Epidote + Plagioclase + Quartz): Epidosite / greenschist facies hydrous retrograded rock; charnockites are strictly high-temperature anhydrous granulites.

Q81: Subsolidus Feldspar Exsolution - Antiperthite Texture

Exam: Geology Paper-II (2021)  |  Authoritative Reference: J.D. Winter (Principles of Igneous and Metamorphic Petrology, Ch. 6, Fig. 6-16)

Part I: Theoretical Foundation & Concept Masterclass

1. Question & Core Mineralogical Identification

Question 81: An inter-growth texture in which plagioclase contains inclusions of potash feldspar is known as :

  • (A) Antiperthite
  • (B) Perthite
  • (C) Graphic texture
  • (D) Ophitic

Correct Answer: (A) Antiperthite

Part II: Official Question & Critical Option Dissection

Q81. An inter-growth texture in which plagioclase contains inclusions of potash feldspar is known as :
(A) Antiperthite
(B) Perthite
(C) Graphic texture
(D) Ophitic

2. Detailed Geological Masterclass: Subsolidus Exsolution in Feldspars

Feldspars form extensive solid solutions at elevated magmatic temperatures ($>700^\circ ext{C}$), but due to differences in ionic radii between potassium ($K^+ = 1.38 ext{ \AA}$) and sodium ($Na^+ = 1.02 ext{ \AA}$), a large solvus exists at subsolidus temperatures. Upon slow cooling through the solvus curve, exsolution occurs:

  • Perthite: Potassium feldspar (orthoclase or microcline) forms the continuous host crystal, containing exsolved blebs, strings, or lamellae of sodic plagioclase (albite). This is common in granite pegmatites and granites.
  • Antiperthite: Plagioclase feldspar (typically oligoclase or andesine) acts as the host mineral, containing oriented exsolved inclusions, patches, or lamellae of potash feldspar. Antiperthite is characteristic of high-grade metamorphic rocks (granulites, charnockites) and some deep-seated plutonic rocks.
  • Graphic Texture: An intergrowth of quartz and K-feldspar resembling runic cuneiform writing, produced by simultaneous eutectic crystallization, not subsolidus exsolution.
  • Ophitic Texture: Laths of plagioclase completely or partially enclosed within larger clinopyroxene (augite) plates, typical of dolerites and gabbros.

Part III: Synthesis Reference Tables & High-Yield Practice

3. Critical Option Elimination & Exam Traps

  • Option A (Antiperthite) is correct: Plagioclase host with exsolved K-feldspar inclusions = Antiperthite.
  • Option B (Perthite): The inverse relationship—potash feldspar is the host containing albite lamellae.
  • Option C (Graphic texture): Quartz-alkali feldspar eutectic intergrowth, not feldspar-in-feldspar exsolution.
  • Option D (Ophitic): Plagioclase in pyroxene magmatic crystallization texture.

Q82: Autometamorphism & Deuteric Alteration in Igneous Rocks

Exam: Geology Paper-II (2021)  |  Authoritative Reference: J.D. Winter (Principles of Igneous and Metamorphic Petrology, Ch. 3, p. 48)

Part I: Theoretical Foundation & Concept Masterclass

1. Question & Conceptual Demarcation

Question 82: Which of the following statements w. r. t. Autometamorphic processes is not correct ?

  • (A) These secondary mineral reactions occur in igneous rocks as they cool, and are not products of a distinct later metamorphic event.
  • (B) These processes are more common in plutonic rocks than in volcanics.
  • (C) Diagenetic and weathering processes are also considered to be Autometamorphic.
  • (D) Most reactions involve minerals at moderate temperatures in an environment in which H₂O is either liberated from residual melt or externally introduced.

Correct Answer: (C) Diagenetic and weathering processes are also considered to be Autometamorphic.

Part II: Official Question & Critical Option Dissection

Q82. Which of the following statements w. r. t. Autometamorphic processes is not correct ?
(A) These secondary mineral reactions occur in igneous rocks as they cool, and are not products of a distinct later metamorphic event.
(B) These processes are more common in plutonic rocks than in volcanics.
(C) Diagenetic and weathering processes are also considered to be Autometamorphic.
(D) Most reactions involve minerals at moderate temperatures in an environment in which H2O is either liberated from residual melt or externally introduced.

2. Detailed Geological Masterclass: Autometamorphism (Deuteric Alteration)

Autometamorphism (frequently termed deuteric alteration) refers to mineral reactions occurring within an igneous body during the late magmatic to post-magmatic cooling stages, driven by hot residual volatile-rich fluids (pneumatolytic and hydrothermal solutions) expelled by the cooling magma itself:

  • Cooling Stage Phenomenon: It is continuous with magmatic consolidation and does not represent an independent or later regional/thermal metamorphic cycle (Statement A is TRUE).
  • Plutonic Dominance: Volatile fluids are trapped and retained under pressure in plutonic settings, whereas volcanic lavas readily degas into the atmosphere; hence autometamorphism is substantially more pervasive in plutonic rocks (Statement B is TRUE).
  • Moderate Temperature Hydrous Reactions: Reactions occur at $300^\circ ext{C}$ to $600^\circ ext{C}$ involving serpentine, chlorite, epidote, uralite, tourmaline, and sericite due to internal/external $H_2O$ and volatile enrichment (Statement D is TRUE).
  • Diagenesis and Weathering are NOT Autometamorphic: Diagenesis occurs at sedimentary burial conditions ($<200^\circ ext{C}$), and weathering is caused by surface atmospheric meteoric agents. Neither is related to igneous crystallization or magmatic cooling (Statement C is FALSE, hence the correct answer).

Part III: Synthesis Reference Tables & High-Yield Practice

3. Critical Option Elimination & Exam Traps

  • Option C is the incorrect statement (hence correct answer): Diagenesis and weathering are exogenous surficial and sedimentary processes, strictly distinct from magmatic autometamorphic reactions.
  • Options A, B, and D are valid petrological truths: They accurately describe autometamorphic / deuteric conditions as defined by Winter and Turner & Verhoogen.

Q83: Himalayan Tectonic Architecture - Main Central Thrust (MCT)

Exam: Geology Paper-II (2021)  |  Authoritative Reference: Van der Pluijm & Marshak (Earth Structure, Ch. 21, Fig. 21.21)

Part I: Theoretical Foundation & Concept Masterclass

1. Question & Tectonic Framework

Question 83: The ductile shear zone along with the High-grade Great Himalayan Crystalline complex was placed above the Low-grade to unmeta-morphosed Lesser Himalayan Sequence is termed as the :

  • (A) Main Central Thrust (MCT)
  • (B) Main Frontal Thrust (MFT)
  • (C) Main Boundary Thrust (MBT)
  • (D) Himalayan Frontal Thrust (HFT)

Correct Answer: (A) Main Central Thrust (MCT)

Part II: Official Question & Critical Option Dissection

Q83. The ductile shear zone along with the High-grade Great Himalayan Crystalline complex was placed above the Low-grade to unmeta-morphosed Lesser Himalayan Sequence is termed as the :
(A) Main Central Thrust (MCT)
(B) Main Frontal Thrust (MFT)
(C) Main Boundary Thrust (MBT)
(D) Himalayan Frontal Thrust (HFT)

2. Detailed Geological Masterclass: Himalayan Tectonic Architecture

The Himalayan orogen was built by the collision of India with Eurasia and is segmented from north to south by major longitudinal fault and thrust systems:

Tectonic Boundary Hanging Wall (North) Footwall (South) Kinematic & Metamorphic Character
STDS (South Tibetan Detachment System) Tethyan Sedimentary Series Higher Himalayan Crystallines North-dipping low-angle normal fault (extensional collapse)
MCT (Main Central Thrust) Higher (Great) Himalayan Crystallines (HHC) Lesser Himalayan Sequence (LHS) Major ductile shear zone; places amphibolite-granulite facies inverted metamorphic rocks over greenschist-grade LHS.
MBT (Main Boundary Thrust) Lesser Himalayan Sequence Sub-Himalayan Siwalik Group Brittle thrust faulting of pre-Tertiary LHS over Neogene molasse.
MFT / HFT (Main / Himalayan Frontal Thrust) Sub-Himalayan Siwaliks Indo-Gangetic Alluvial Plain Active southernmost blind/emergent thrust fault separating Siwaliks from the foreland basin.

Part III: Synthesis Reference Tables & High-Yield Practice

3. Critical Option Elimination & Exam Traps

  • Option A (MCT) is correct: The MCT is the definitive boundary placing the High-grade Great Himalayan Crystalline complex over the Lesser Himalayan Sequence.
  • Option B & D (MFT / HFT): The frontal thrust between the Siwalik hills and the Indo-Gangetic alluvium.
  • Option C (MBT): The boundary between the Lesser Himalaya and the Sub-Himalaya (Siwaliks).

Q84: Forms of Igneous Intrusions - Bysmalith (Fault-Bounded Cylindrical Pluton)

Exam: Geology Paper-II (2021)  |  Authoritative Reference: K.M. Bangar (Principles of Engineering Geology, Ch. 5, p. 168–170)

Part I: Theoretical Foundation & Concept Masterclass

1. Question & Structural Definition

Question 84: An igneous pluton which is more or less vertical and cylindrical that cross-cuts adjacent sediments and is bounded by steep faults is termed as :

  • (A) Laccolith
  • (B) Bysmalith
  • (C) Lopolith
  • (D) Conolith

Correct Answer: (B) Bysmalith

Part II: Official Question & Critical Option Dissection

Q84. An igneous pluton which is more or less vertical and cylindrical that cross-cuts adjacent sediments and is bounded by steep faults is termed as :
(A) Laccolith
(B) Bysmalith
(C) Lopolith
(D) Conolith

2. Detailed Geological Masterclass: Concordant vs Discordant Intrusive Forms

Igneous intrusions are classified based on their geometry and relationship to host bedding:

  • Bysmalith: A term introduced by J.P. Iddings (1898) to denote a specialized form of laccolith where the upward-moving magma has punched vertically like a cylindrical piston, cross-cutting the country rocks and bounded on its sides by steep circular faults or shear fractures.
  • Laccolith: A concordant, dome-shaped or mushroom-shaped intrusion with a flat floor and convex-up roof that arches overlying sedimentary strata without cylindrical peripheral fault cut-offs.
  • Lopolith: A massive saucer-shaped or basin-shaped concordant intrusion with a sunken central floor (e.g., Bushveld Complex, Duluth Complex).
  • Conolith: An irregular, cone-shaped discordant intrusive body lacking systematic geometric symmetry.

Part III: Synthesis Reference Tables & High-Yield Practice

3. Critical Option Elimination & Exam Traps

  • Option B (Bysmalith) is correct: Steep-fault bounded, vertical, cylindrical punched plug matching Iddings' classic definition.
  • Option A (Laccolith): Lacks steep bounding faults; concordant mushroom dome.
  • Option C (Lopolith): Basin-shaped / saucer-shaped concordant intrusion.
  • Option D (Conolith): Cone-like discordant intrusion without cylindrical fault-bounded architecture.

Q85: Lamprophyre Petrography - Panidiomorphic Texture

Exam: Geology Paper-II (2021)  |  Authoritative Reference: K.M. Bangar (Principles of Engineering Geology, Ch. 5, p. 165, 178); Winter (Ch. 2)

Part I: Theoretical Foundation & Concept Masterclass

1. Question & Petrological Identification

Question 85: The characteristic texture of lamprophyres is :

  • (A) Allotriomorphic
  • (B) Panidiomorphic
  • (C) Xenomorphic
  • (D) Hypidiomorphic

Correct Answer: (B) Panidiomorphic

Part II: Official Question & Critical Option Dissection

Q85. The characteristic texture of lamprophyres is :
(A) Allotriomorphic
(B) Panidiomorphic
(C) Xenomorphic
(D) Hypidiomorphic

2. Detailed Geological Masterclass: Lamprophyric & Panidiomorphic Textures

Lamprophyres are melanocratic, porphyritic, volatile-rich hypabyssal dyke rocks containing abundant phenocrysts of mafic minerals (biotite, phlogopite, amphibole, or pyroxene) and devoid of felsic phenocrysts (feldspars and feldspathoids are strictly confined to the groundmass).

  • Panidiomorphic Texture: A texture in which nearly all mineral components, both in the phenocryst and matrix generations, show well-formed, idiomorphic (euhedral) crystal boundaries. In lamprophyres, this is often called the lamprophyric texture.
  • Hypidiomorphic (Granitic) Texture: Subhedral texture with some minerals showing crystal faces and others anhedral, standard for granites and diorites.
  • Allotriomorphic / Xenomorphic Texture: A texture where virtually all mineral grains are anhedral (lacking crystal faces), typical of aplites and quartzites.

Part III: Synthesis Reference Tables & High-Yield Practice

3. Critical Option Elimination & Exam Traps

  • Option B (Panidiomorphic) is correct: Textbook diagnostic hallmark of all lamprophyres.
  • Option A & C (Allotriomorphic / Xenomorphic): Completely anhedral grains; characteristic of aplites (aplitic texture), opposite of lamprophyres.
  • Option D (Hypidiomorphic): Partially euhedral, common in plutonic rocks like granite, not the exclusive hallmark of lamprophyres.

Q86: Petrochemical Classification - Monomineralic vs Ultrabasic Rocks (Anorthosite)

Exam: Geology Paper-II (2021)  |  Authoritative Reference: J.D. Winter (Principles of Igneous and Metamorphic Petrology, Ch. 2, p. 29); Bangar (p. 79)

Part I: Theoretical Foundation & Concept Masterclass

1. Question & Petrochemical Classification

Question 86: Which of the following is not a monomineralic ultrabasic rock ?

  • (A) Anorthosite
  • (B) Pyroxinite
  • (C) Leptynite
  • (D) Dunite

Correct Answer: (A) Anorthosite

Part II: Official Question & Critical Option Dissection

Q86. Which of the following is not a monomineralic ultrabasic rock ?
(A) Anorthosite
(B) Pyroxinite
(C) Leptynite
(D) Dunite

2. Detailed Geological Masterclass: Monomineralic vs Ultrabasic Rocks

In igneous and metamorphic petrology, rock classifications depend on silica percentage ($SiO_2$) and modal mineral proportions:

  • Chemical Classification by Silica:
    • Ultrabasic: $SiO_2 < 45\%$, very rich in $Mg, Fe, Ca$ (e.g., Dunite, Pyroxenite, Peridotite).
    • Basic: $SiO_2 = 45 ext{--}52\%$ (Gabbro, Basalt, Anorthosite).
    • Intermediate: $SiO_2 = 52 ext{--}66\%$ (Diorite, Andesite).
    • Acidic: $SiO_2 > 66\%$ (Granite, Rhyolite).
  • Monomineralic Rocks: Rocks composed predominantly of a single mineral ($>90\%$):
    • Dunite: $>90\%$ Olivine $ ightarrow$ Monomineralic and Ultrabasic ($SiO_2 pprox 40\%$).
    • Pyroxenite: $>90\%$ Pyroxene $ ightarrow$ Monomineralic and Ultrabasic ($SiO_2 pprox 44 ext{--}48\%$).
    • Anorthosite: $>90\%$ Plagioclase feldspar $ ightarrow$ Monomineralic but NOT ultrabasic; it is a basic-to-felsic rock ($SiO_2 = 48 ext{--}55\%$, rich in $Al_2O_3$ and $CaO/Na_2O$).
  • Note on Leptynite: Leptynite is a granulitic metamorphic rock consisting of quartz, feldspar, and garnet (a polymineralic acid granulite). In standard Indian geology question banks (e.g., Bangar, Mahapatra), Anorthosite is universally taught as the prime example of a monomineralic rock that is not ultrabasic.

Part III: Synthesis Reference Tables & High-Yield Practice

3. Critical Option Elimination & Exam Traps

  • Option A (Anorthosite) is correct: Anorthosite is composed of $\ge 90\%$ plagioclase, making it monomineralic, but it is basic/felsic ($SiO_2 > 45\%$, high $Al_2O_3$), NOT ultrabasic.
  • Option B (Pyroxinite): Monomineralic ultrabasic rock composed of $>90\%$ pyroxene.
  • Option D (Dunite): Monomineralic ultrabasic rock composed of $>90\%$ olivine.
  • Option C (Leptynite): Granulite-facies metamorphic rock (polymineralic quartzo-feldspathic gneiss).

Q87: Alkaline Foid Plutonites - Fergusite (Pseudoleucite-Pyroxene Rock)

Exam: Geology Paper-II (2021)  |  Authoritative Reference: J.D. Winter (Principles of Igneous and Metamorphic Petrology, Ch. 2, p. 28); Le Maitre (2002)

Part I: Theoretical Foundation & Concept Masterclass

1. Question & Alkaline Rock Petrography

Question 87: The plutonic rock consisting of roughly 70% pseudoleucite (alkali feldspar, nepheline, kalsilite and minor analcime) and 30% pyroxene is termed as :

  • (A) Ferrilite
  • (B) Fenite
  • (C) Fergusite
  • (D) Felsite

Correct Answer: (C) Fergusite

Part II: Official Question & Critical Option Dissection

Q87. The plutonic rock consisting of roughly 70% pseudoleucite (alkali feldspar, nepheline, kalsilite and minor analcime) and 30% pyroxene is termed as :
(A) Ferrilite
(B) Fenite
(C) Fergusite
(D) Felsite

2. Detailed Geological Masterclass: Alkaline & Foid-Bearing Plutonites

In the IUGS nomenclature of highly potassic and silica-undersaturated alkaline rocks:

  • Fergusite: A rare foid-bearing plutonic rock composed predominantly of pseudoleucite (typically $pprox 70\%$) and clinopyroxene (typically aegirine-augite, $pprox 30\%$), named after Fergus County, Montana. Pseudoleucite represents subsolidus breakdown aggregates of leucite into K-feldspar + nepheline/kalsilite.
  • Fenite: A metasomatic rock produced by high-temperature alkali metasomatism (fenitization) of granitic or gneissic country rocks surrounding carbonatite or alkaline intrusions.
  • Felsite: A field or petrographic term for very fine-grained, light-colored (felsic) volcanic or hypabyssal rocks (composed of quartz and feldspar).
  • Ferrilite: An obsolete or localized term for iron-rich sedimentary or volcanic rocks.

Part III: Synthesis Reference Tables & High-Yield Practice

3. Critical Option Elimination & Exam Traps

  • Option C (Fergusite) is correct: Precisely matches the IUGS definition: $70\%$ pseudoleucite and $30\%$ pyroxene.
  • Option B (Fenite): Metasomatic rock aureole around carbonatites, not a primary pseudoleucite plutonic rock.
  • Option D (Felsite): Fine-grained light-colored volcanic rock.
  • Option A (Ferrilite): Non-existent in IUGS alkaline classification.

Q88: IUGS QAPF Classification - Field 8* Quartz Monzonite

Exam: Geology Paper-II (2021)  |  Authoritative Reference: J.D. Winter (Principles of Igneous and Metamorphic Petrology, Ch. 2, p. 28)

Part I: Theoretical Foundation & Concept Masterclass

1. Question & IUGS QAPF Classification

Question 88: A plutonic rock consisting of approximately equal amounts of alkali feldspar and plagioclase and with essential quartz (5%-20% of felsic minerals) but not enough to make the rock a granite is termed as :

  • (A) Quartz Monzonite
  • (B) Quartz Monzodiorite
  • (C) Quartz Norite
  • (D) Quartz Monzogabbro

Correct Answer: (A) Quartz Monzonite

Part II: Official Question & Critical Option Dissection

Q88. A plutonic rock consisting of approximately equal amounts of alkali feldspar and plagioclase and with essential quartz (5%-20% of felsic minerals) but not enough to make the rock a granite is termed as :
(A) Quartz Monzonite
(B) Quartz Monzodiorite
(C) Quartz Norite
(D) Quartz Monzogabbro

2. Detailed Geological Masterclass: The IUGS QAPF Plutonic Classification

The International Union of Geological Sciences (IUGS) classifies plutonic rocks using modal proportions of Quartz (Q), Alkali Feldspar (A), and Plagioclase (P):

  • Field 8 (Monzonite): $P/(A+P) = 35 ext{--}65\%$ (equal feldspars), with $Q < 5\%$ and $F < 10\%$.
  • Field 8* (Quartz Monzonite): $P/(A+P) = 35 ext{--}65\%$ (approximately equal amounts of alkali feldspar and plagioclase), with quartz content between $5\%$ and $20\%$ of total felsic minerals.
  • Field 3 (Granite): Requires quartz content $Q > 20\%$ (20–60% Q). Hence, 5–20% Q is explicitly "not enough to make the rock a granite".
  • Quartz Monzodiorite / Quartz Monzogabbro (Field 9*): Dominated by plagioclase where $P/(A+P) = 65 ext{--}90\%$.

Part III: Synthesis Reference Tables & High-Yield Practice

3. Critical Option Elimination & Exam Traps

  • Option A (Quartz Monzonite) is correct: Equal alkali feldspar and plagioclase ($35 ext{--}65\%$) with 5–20% quartz is the exact definition of Field 8*.
  • Option B & D (Quartz Monzodiorite / Monzogabbro): Plagioclase heavily dominates over alkali feldspar ($P/(A+P) > 65\%$).
  • Option C (Quartz Norite): Hypersthene-bearing gabbroic rock dominated almost entirely by calcic plagioclase ($P/(A+P) > 90\%$).

(D) Clinopyroxene + plagioclase

2. Detailed Geological Masterclass: IUGS Peridotite Classification

Ultramafic rocks containing $>40\%$ olivine are called peridotites, and are categorized on the Olivine - Orthopyroxene - Clinopyroxene ternary diagram:

Rock Name Essential Minerals Mantle / Ophiolite Significance
Dunite $>90\%$ Olivine Extreme refractory mantle residue / cumulate
Harzburgite Olivine + Orthopyroxene (enstatite) ($<10\%$ Cpx) Depleted residual mantle peridotite (dominant in ophiolite mantle sections)
Wehrlite Olivine + Clinopyroxene (diopside) ($<10\%$ Opx) Cumulate peridotite / metasomatized mantle
Lherzolite Olivine + Orthopyroxene + Clinopyroxene Fertile, primitive upper mantle composition

Part III: Synthesis Reference Tables & High-Yield Practice

  • Option A (Olivine + orthopyroxene) is correct: Harzburgite is strictly defined as an orthopyroxene-peridotite.
  • Option B (Olivine + clinopyroxene): Defines wehrlite.
  • Option C (Olivine + plagioclase): Defines troctolite (mafic gabbroic rock, not ultramafic peridotite).
  • Option D (Clinopyroxene + plagioclase): Defines standard gabbro.

  • (A) Anorthosite

Part II: Official Question & Critical Option Dissection

Q90. An intermediate volcanic rock, usually porphyritic, consisting of plagioclase (frequently zoned from labradorite to oligoclase), pyroxene, hornblende and/or biotite is termed as :
(A) Anorthosite
(B) Andesite

(D) Andesinite

2. Detailed Geological Masterclass: Andesite Petrology

Andesite is the quintessential intermediate volcanic rock ($SiO_2 = 52 ext{--}63\%$) named after the Andes mountain chain, where it erupts at destructive continental subduction margins:

  • Texture: Typically porphyritic with fine-grained or glassy groundmass.
  • Mineralogy: Phenocrysts are dominated by plagioclase feldspar exhibiting spectacular oscillatory normal zoning (ranging from calcic cores of labradorite to sodic rims of oligoclase/andesine), accompanied by hornblende, augite, hypersthene, and/or biotite.
  • Distinctions:
    • Anorthosite is a coarse-grained plutonic rock consisting almost entirely ($>90\%$) of plagioclase.
    • Andesitoid and Andesinite are non-standard or obsolete terms.

Part III: Synthesis Reference Tables & High-Yield Practice

3. Critical Option Elimination & Exam Traps

  • Option B (Andesite) is correct: The textbook definition of intermediate porphyritic volcanic rock with zoned plagioclase and mafic minerals.
  • Option A (Anorthosite): Plutonic, monomineralic plagioclase rock ($>90\%$ plagioclase).
  • Option C & D (Andesitoid / Andesinite): Distractors not recognized in standard IUGS volcanic nomenclature.

Q91: Sandstone Classification - Argillaceous Sandstone and Clay Matrix

Exam: Geology Paper-II (2021)  |  Authoritative Reference: Sam Boggs Jr. (Principles of Sedimentology and Stratigraphy, Ch. 5, p. 145)

Part I: Theoretical Foundation & Concept Masterclass

1. Question & Sedimentary Classification

Question 91: Cementing material differs in different sandstones, the sandstone where cementing material is clay is named :

  • (A) Ferruginous sandstone
  • (B) Argillaceous sandstone
  • (C) Calcareous sandstone
  • (D) Siliceous sandstone

Correct Answer: (B) Argillaceous sandstone

Part II: Official Question & Critical Option Dissection

Q91. Cementing material differs in different sandstones, the sandstone where cementing material is clay is named :
(A) Ferruginous sandstone
(B) Argillaceous sandstone
(C) Calcareous sandstone
(D) Siliceous sandstone

2. Detailed Geological Masterclass: Sandstone Cements and Classification

Sandstones consist of framework grains (sand size: $0.0625 ext{--}2.0 ext{ mm}$) bound together by mineral cement or matrix:

  • Argillaceous Sandstone: The interstitial matrix/cement is composed predominantly of clay minerals (kaolinite, illite, chlorite, or smectite). The rock is softer, often earthy, and fractures irregularly.
  • Siliceous Sandstone: Sand grains are cemented by silica (secondary quartz overgrowths, chalcedony, or opal). This produces extremely tough, durable sandstones that often grade into orthoquartzite.
  • Calcareous Sandstone: Grains are cemented by carbonate minerals, primarily calcite or dolomite, which effervesces readily in dilute hydrochloric acid ($HCl$).
  • Ferruginous Sandstone: Cement consists of iron oxides or hydroxides (hematite, goethite, limonite), giving the rock a characteristic red, brown, or yellow coloration.

Part III: Synthesis Reference Tables & High-Yield Practice

3. Critical Option Elimination & Exam Traps

  • Option B (Argillaceous sandstone) is correct: Derived from Latin argilla (clay); sandstone cemented by clay.
  • Option A (Ferruginous sandstone): Cemented by iron oxide minerals.
  • Option C (Calcareous sandstone): Cemented by calcium carbonate ($CaCO_3$).
  • Option D (Siliceous sandstone): Cemented by silica ($SiO_2$).

Correct Answer: (B) laminar structure

Part II: Official Question & Critical Option Dissection

Q92. Shales are generally characterized with distinct :
(A) cleavage
(B) laminar structure
(C) joints
(D) parting

2. Detailed Geological Masterclass: Shale Petrology and Lamination

Shale is a fine-grained siliciclastic sedimentary rock composed of silt- and clay-sized particles ($<0.0625 ext{ mm}$).

  • Laminar Structure & Fissility: The defining physical characteristic of shale is its finely laminated depositional bedding (laminae $<10 ext{ mm}$ thick) and its tendency to split easily along these parallel bedding planes (fissility). This laminar structure arises from the parallel sedimentation and subsequent compaction of platy phyllosilicate clay minerals (illite, kaolinite, smectite).
  • Cleavage: A tectonic deformational feature produced by metamorphic recrystallization under directed stress (e.g., slaty cleavage in slate), not an inherent primary sedimentary structure of unmetamorphosed shales.
  • Parting & Joints: Secondary structural planes that occur in all rock types, not the diagnostic feature of shale.

Part III: Synthesis Reference Tables & High-Yield Practice

3. Critical Option Elimination & Exam Traps

  • Option B (laminar structure) is correct: Shales are textbook-defined by their distinct laminar structure and fissility.
  • Option A (cleavage): Metamorphic rock property (slate/phyllite).
  • Option C & D (joints / parting): Universal rock mechanical fracture properties, not diagnostic of shale petrogenesis.

Q93: Sedimentary Rock Genesis - Clastic Rocks from Mechanical Breakdown

Exam: Geology Paper-II (2021)  |  Authoritative Reference: Sam Boggs Jr. (Principles of Sedimentology and Stratigraphy, Ch. 5, p. 130)

Part I: Theoretical Foundation & Concept Masterclass

1. Question & Sedimentary Classification

Question 93: Sedimentary rocks formed due to the sediments formed from mechanical breakdown of primary rocks is called :

  • (A) siliclastic rocks
  • (B) clastic rocks
  • (C) semi-clastic rocks
  • (D) chemical sediments

Correct Answer: (B) clastic rocks

Part II: Official Question & Critical Option Dissection

Q93. Sedimentary rocks formed due to the sediments formed from mechanical breakdown of primary rocks is called :
(A) siliclastic rocks
(B) clastic rocks
(C) semi-clastic rocks
(D) chemical sediments

2. Detailed Geological Masterclass: Clastic vs Non-Clastic Rocks

Sedimentary rocks are divided into two fundamental genetic divisions:

  • Clastic (Detrital) Sedimentary Rocks: Formed from discrete fragments (clasts, from Greek klastos = broken) produced by the physical/mechanical breakdown, weathering, and erosion of pre-existing rocks (igneous, metamorphic, or older sedimentary), transported mechanically and lithified. Examples: conglomerate, breccia, sandstone, siltstone, shale.
  • Non-Clastic Sedimentary Rocks: Formed through chemical precipitation from solution (e.g., halite, gypsum, limestone) or biological accumulation of organic skeletal remains (e.g., chalk, coal, diatomite).
  • Siliciclastic: A sub-class of clastic rocks where the detrital clasts are rich in silicate minerals (quartz, feldspar). "Clastic rocks" is the broad, fundamental parent category defined by mechanical breakdown.

Part III: Synthesis Reference Tables & High-Yield Practice

3. Critical Option Elimination & Exam Traps

  • Option B (clastic rocks) is correct: The broad, foundational genetic term for rocks produced by mechanical breakdown of pre-existing rocks.
  • Option A (siliclastic rocks): A narrower compositional subset; does not cover carbonate clastic rocks (calcarenites, bioclasts).
  • Option C (semi-clastic rocks): Non-standard descriptive term.
  • Option D (chemical sediments): Formed by precipitation from aqueous solutions, not mechanical disintegration.

Q94: Weathering Geomorphology - Spheroidal Weathering along Joint Networks

Exam: Geology Paper-II (2021)  |  Authoritative Reference: K.M. Bangar (Principles of Engineering Geology, Ch. 2, p. 28)

Part I: Theoretical Foundation & Concept Masterclass

1. Question & Weathering Geomorphology

Question 94: A type of exfoliation due to weathering that produces rounded features when chemical weathering moves along joints in the bed is called :

  • (A) spheroidal weathering
  • (B) frost wedging
  • (C) mechanical weathering
  • (D) Both (A) and (C) are correct

Correct Answer: (A) spheroidal weathering

Part II: Official Question & Critical Option Dissection

Q94. A type of exfoliation due to weathering that produces rounded features when chemical weathering moves along joints in the bed is called :
(A) spheroidal weathering
(B) frost wedging
(C) mechanical weathering
(D) Both (A) and (C) are correct

2. Detailed Geological Masterclass: Spheroidal Weathering

Spheroidal weathering (concentric weathering) is a form of chemical weathering that attacks jointed massive bedrock (especially granites, basalts, and dolerites):

  • Geometric Mechanism: Water carrying dissolved carbonic and organic acids penetrates joint networks, intersecting at sharp corners and edges. A corner is attacked from three perpendicular directions simultaneously, an edge from two directions, and a planar face from only one direction.
  • Rounding Effect: Consequently, corners and edges decompose much more rapidly than planar faces, converting rectangular/orthogonal joint blocks into rounded boulders surrounded by concentric shells of decayed rock (spall sheets / onion-skin exfoliation).
  • Frost Wedging & Mechanical Weathering: Purely physical processes driven by ice expansion ($9\%$ volume increase) or thermal stress, which produce angular, sharp talus fragments, not smooth rounded boulders via joint-controlled chemical alteration.

Part III: Synthesis Reference Tables & High-Yield Practice

3. Critical Option Elimination & Exam Traps

  • Option A (spheroidal weathering) is correct: Specifically defined by chemical weathering penetrating orthogonal joints to produce rounded boulders and concentric spalls.
  • Option B (frost wedging): Mechanical frost-shattering producing sharp, angular scree.
  • Option C & D: The question specifically stipulates that "chemical weathering moves along joints", which defines spheroidal weathering, not pure mechanical weathering.

Q95: Karst Geomorphology - Carbonate Bedrock and Dissolution Features

Exam: Geology Paper-II (2021)  |  Authoritative Reference: K.M. Bangar (Principles of Engineering Geology, Ch. 2, p. 64–66)

Part I: Theoretical Foundation & Concept Masterclass

1. Question & Karst Geomorphology

Question 95: Karst topography is a special type of landform characterized by sinkholes or caves, developed in :

  • (A) Calcareous sandstone
  • (B) Shales
  • (C) Carbonate bedrock
  • (D) Basaltic beds

Correct Answer: (C) Carbonate bedrock

Part II: Official Question & Critical Option Dissection

Q95. Karst topography is a special type of landform characterized by sinkholes or caves, developed in :
(A) Calcareous sandstone
(B) Shales
(C) Carbonate bedrock
(D) Basaltic beds

2. Detailed Geological Masterclass: Karst Hydrogeology and Carbonate Dissolution

Karst topography is a distinctive landscape formed from the dissolution of soluble rocks, overwhelmingly dominated by carbonate bedrock (limestone, $CaCO_3$, and dolostone, $CaMg(CO_3)_2$):

  • Dissolution Chemistry: Atmospheric and soil water absorbs carbon dioxide to form carbonic acid: $$ ext{H}_2 ext{O} + ext{CO}_2 ightleftharpoons ext{H}_2 ext{CO}_3$$ $$ ext{CaCO}_3 ext{ (calcite)} + ext{H}_2 ext{CO}_3 ightleftharpoons ext{Ca}^{2+} + 2 ext{HCO}_3^-$$
  • Diagnostic Landforms:
    • Surface Features: Sinkholes (dolines), uvalas, poljes, grikes and clints (lapies), sinking streams (swallow holes / ponors), and karst valleys.
    • Subsurface Features: Extensive cave systems, subterranean rivers, stalactites, stalagmites, and flowstones.
  • Insoluble Bedrocks: Shales and basalts are silicate-dominated and do not undergo rapid congruent carbonic acid solution; hence karst topography cannot develop within them.

Part III: Synthesis Reference Tables & High-Yield Practice

3. Critical Option Elimination & Exam Traps

  • Option C (Carbonate bedrock) is correct: Karst terrain universally develops in massive, jointed limestone and dolomite bedrock.
  • Option A (Calcareous sandstone): Has carbonate cement but quartz framework prevents extensive continuous cave/sinkhole network formation.
  • Option B (Shales) & Option D (Basaltic beds): Insoluble silicate rocks incapable of karst development.

Q96: Paleoclimatic Sedimentary Indicators - Continental Red Beds in Arid Climates

1. Question & Paleoclimatic Sedimentary Indicators

Question 96: Sedimentary rocks that are formed in arid climatic condition are classified as :

  • (A) Ironstone
  • (B) Red beds
  • (C) Cherty sandstone
  • (D) All of these

Correct Answer: (B) Red beds

Part II: Official Question & Critical Option Dissection

Q96. Sedimentary rocks that are formed in arid climatic condition are classified as :
(A) Ironstone
(B) Red beds
(C) Cherty sandstone
(D) All of these

2. Detailed Geological Masterclass: Continental Red Beds & Arid Paleoclimates

Red beds are sequence of continental siliciclastic sedimentary rocks (sandstones, siltstones, conglomerates, and mudstones) that possess a distinctive red, reddish-brown, or purple coloration due to microscopic coatings and pigments of ferric oxide (principally hematite, $ ext{Fe}_2 ext{O}_3$):

  • Arid / Semi-Arid Depositional Setting: Red beds form in oxidizing continental environments such as alluvial fans, desert dunes (aeolian ergs), playa lake margins, and arid fluvial floodplains. The dry, oxidizing conditions prevent the reduction of iron into soluble ferrous ($Fe^{2+}$) forms or preservation of organic plant carbon.
  • Diagenetic Pigmentation: In warm, oxidizing, arid groundwaters, detrital iron-bearing silicates (hornblende, pyroxene, biotite) break down to release iron, which crystallizes as ultra-fine hematite pigments coating quartz and feldspar grains.
  • Ironstones: Typically marine sedimentary iron deposits formed under fluctuating redox conditions, not diagnostic of continental aridity.

Part III: Synthesis Reference Tables & High-Yield Practice

3. Critical Option Elimination & Exam Traps

  • Option B (Red beds) is correct: Classical sedimentary lithofacies used globally as an unequivocal indicator of continental arid to semi-arid paleoclimates (e.g., Old Red Sandstone, New Red Sandstone).
  • Option A (Ironstone): Marine chemical/biochemical iron deposit.
  • Option C (Cherty sandstone): Siliceous sandstone formed in varied environments, not an arid paleoclimate indicator.

Q97: Chemical Sedimentary Rocks - Evaporite Gypsum Formation

Exam: Geology Paper-II (2021)  |  Authoritative Reference: Sam Boggs Jr. (Principles of Sedimentology and Stratigraphy, Ch. 7, Table 7.1)

Part I: Theoretical Foundation & Concept Masterclass

Question 97: ——— is an example of Chemical Sedimentary Rock.

  • (A) Breccia
  • (B) Laterite
  • (C) Bauxite

Correct Answer: (D) Gypsum

Part II: Official Question & Critical Option Dissection

Q97. ——— is an example of Chemical Sedimentary Rock.
(A) Breccia
(B) Laterite
(C) Bauxite
(D) Gypsum

2. Detailed Geological Masterclass: Evaporites and Chemical Sedimentary Rocks

Sedimentary rocks are categorized by origin into clastic, chemical, biogenic, and residual types:

  • Chemical Sedimentary Rocks: Formed by inorganic chemical precipitation of dissolved mineral salts from water bodies (marine or lacustrine) due to supersaturation and evaporation:
    • Gypsum ($ ext{CaSO}_4 \cdot 2 ext{H}_2 ext{O}$): A primary chemical evaporite that precipitates when seawater is concentrated to roughly $19\%$ of its original volume (after calcite and before halite).
    • Other chemical rocks include halite (rock salt), anhydrite, and chemical chert.
  • Breccia: A coarse-grained clastic sedimentary rock composed of angular, broken fragments ($>2 ext{ mm}$) cemented in a fine-grained matrix.
  • Laterite & Bauxite: Residual soils / weathering crusts (duricrusts) formed by intense in-situ subaerial leaching of silica in humid tropical climates, not precipitated chemical sedimentary rocks.

Part III: Synthesis Reference Tables & High-Yield Practice

3. Critical Option Elimination & Exam Traps

  • Option D (Gypsum) is correct: True chemical evaporite sedimentary rock precipitated from saline brines.
  • Option A (Breccia): Clastic / mechanical sedimentary rock with angular fragments.
  • Option B & C (Laterite / Bauxite): Residual chemical weathering profiles (paleosols), not sedimentary chemical strata.

Q98: Sedimentary Processes - Diagenesis vs Lithification

Exam: Geology Paper-II (2021)  |  Authoritative Reference: Sam Boggs Jr. (Principles of Sedimentology and Stratigraphy, Ch. 8, p. 180)

Part I: Theoretical Foundation & Concept Masterclass

1. Question & Post-Depositional Processes

Question 98: The physical or chemical transformation of sediments or soil by geological processes is termed as :

  • (A) Diagenesis
  • (B) Petrogenesis
  • (C) Lithification
  • (D) Crustificaton

Correct Answer: (A) Diagenesis

Part II: Official Question & Critical Option Dissection

Q98. The physical or chemical transformation of sediments or soil by geological processes is termed as :
(A) Diagenesis
(B) Petrogenesis
(C) Lithification
(D) Crustificaton

2. Detailed Geological Masterclass: Diagenesis vs Lithification

Diagenesis encompasses the entire collective suite of physical, chemical, and biological processes that transform unconsolidated sediment or soil following deposition, through shallow and deep burial, up to the boundary of low-grade metamorphism ($T pprox 200^\circ ext{C}$, $P pprox 1 ext{--}2 ext{ kbar}$):

  • Major Diagenetic Processes:
    1. Compaction: Mechanical rearrangement of framework grains under overburden pressure, reducing porosity and expelling interstitial water.
    2. Cementation: Chemical precipitation of mineral phases (quartz, calcite, hematite) into pore spaces, binding clasts together.
    3. Dissolution: Leaching of unstable framework grains (feldspars, carbonate shells) creating secondary porosity.
    4. Authigenesis & Recrystallization: In-situ crystallization of new diagenetic minerals (zeolites, illite, chlorite) and recrystallization of aragonite to calcite.
  • Lithification: A specific sub-process of diagenesis that converts loose sediment strictly into solid coherent rock (primarily compaction + cementation). Diagenesis is the broader, overarching geological term for all physical and chemical transformations.
  • Petrogenesis: The study of the origin and evolution of rocks in general (including igneous magmatic differentiation and high-grade metamorphism).

Part III: Synthesis Reference Tables & High-Yield Practice

3. Critical Option Elimination & Exam Traps

  • Option A (Diagenesis) is correct: The comprehensive geological term for all post-depositional physical and chemical modifications of sediments.
  • Option B (Petrogenesis): Broad science of rock origin across all realms.
  • Option C (Lithification): Subset of diagenesis referring only to hardening/solidification.
  • Option D (Crustification): Hydrothermal vein texture where mineral crusts line cavity walls.

Q99: Textural and Mineralogical Maturity - ZTR Index and Alumina Enrichment

Exam: Geology Paper-II (2021)  |  Authoritative Reference: Sam Boggs Jr. (Principles of Sedimentology and Stratigraphy, Ch. 5, p. 140)

Part I: Theoretical Foundation & Concept Masterclass

1. Question & Sedimentary Maturity Index

Question 99: High SiO₂, Al₂O₃, rounded clasts and high ZTR index indicate _____ maturity of sediments.

  • (A) low
  • (B) high
  • (C) moderate
  • (D) None of these

Correct Answer: (B) high

Part II: Official Question & Critical Option Dissection

Q99. High SiO2, Al2O3, rounded clasts and high ZTR index indicate _____ maturity of sediments.
(A) low
(B) high
(C) moderate
(D) None of these

2. Detailed Geological Masterclass: Textural and Mineralogical Maturity

Sediment maturity describes the degree to which a sediment has evolved from its initial bedrock breakdown state toward a stable, resistant end-member through progressive weathering and transport:

  • Textural Maturity (Folk's Stages): Evolving from immature (high clay matrix) $ ightarrow$ submature $ ightarrow$ mature $ ightarrow$ supermature (well-sorted, matrix-free, and composed of well-rounded clasts from prolonged abrasion).
  • Mineralogical Maturity:
    • High $SiO_2$: Refinement toward pure quartz, the most chemically and mechanically durable common framework silicate.
    • High $Al_2O_3$: Complete breakdown of unstable feldspars into aluminum-rich stable clay residues.
    • ZTR Index (Hubert, 1962): The percentage of ultra-stable non-opaque heavy minerals: $$ ext{ZTR Index} = rac{ ext{Zircon} + ext{Tourmaline} + ext{Rutile}}{\sum( ext{Non-opaque Tourmaline/Zircon/Rutile + other transparent heavies})} imes 100$$ A high ZTR index ($>75\%$) confirms that unstable heavy minerals (pyroxenes, amphiboles, olivine) have been completely leached away, proving high mineralogical maturity.

Part III: Synthesis Reference Tables & High-Yield Practice

3. Critical Option Elimination & Exam Traps

  • Option B (high) is correct: High quartz, alumina, roundness, and high ZTR index are the definitive indicators of high sedimentary maturity.
  • Option A (low): Low maturity sediments (e.g., greywackes, arkoses) have angular grains, low ZTR, and abundant unstable rock fragments and feldspars.
  • Option C (moderate): Submature/intermediate stage.

Q100: Granulometric Analysis - Grain Size Distribution and Frequency Parameters

Exam: Geology Paper-II (2021)  |  Authoritative Reference: Sam Boggs Jr. (Principles of Sedimentology and Stratigraphy, Ch. 3, p. 60)

Part I: Theoretical Foundation & Concept Masterclass

1. Question & Granulometric Methodology

Question 100: An analysis that helps to determine grain size and percentage of the individual size fractions in the specific sediment sample is called :

  • (A) Granulometric analysis
  • (B) Gravimetric analysis
  • (C) Sedimentation analysis
  • (D) Both (A) and (B) are correct

Correct Answer: (A) Granulometric analysis

Part II: Official Question & Critical Option Dissection

Q100. An analysis that helps to determine grain size and percentage of the individual size fractions in the specific sediment sample is called :
(A) Granulometric analysis
(B) Gravimetric analysis
(C) Sedimentation analysis
(D) Both (A) and (B) are correct

2. Detailed Geological Masterclass: Granulometric Analysis (Grain Size Analysis)

Granulometric analysis (or mechanical grain-size analysis) is the fundamental quantitative procedure used by sedimentologists to determine the grain size frequency distribution and the percentage of individual size classes in a clastic sediment sample:

  • Techniques Used:
    • Sieve Analysis: Using a nested stack of standard wire-mesh sieves (Wentworth / Udden phi scale intervals, $\phi = -\log_2 d$) for coarse sand and gravel fractions ($>0.0625 ext{ mm}$).
    • Pipette / Hydrometer Method: Based on Stokes' Law settling velocity for silt and clay mud fractions ($<0.0625 ext{ mm}$).
    • Laser Diffraction / Settling Tubes: Modern automated instrumentation.
  • Output & Statistical Parameters: Produces cumulative frequency curves and histograms, allowing calculation of graphic median ($Md$), mean ($M_z$), sorting (inclusive graphic standard deviation $\sigma_I$), skewness ($Sk_I$), and kurtosis ($K_G$).
  • Gravimetric Analysis: An analytical chemistry technique measuring mass or change in mass to quantify analyte concentration, not grain size distributions.
  • Sedimentation Analysis: While sedimentation settling is one method used to measure fine particles, the overarching scientific analysis to determine grain size distribution across all fractions is Granulometric analysis.

Part III: Synthesis Reference Tables & High-Yield Practice

3. Critical Option Elimination & Exam Traps

  • Option A (Granulometric analysis) is correct: The universal sedimentological term for grain size distribution analysis.
  • Option B (Gravimetric analysis): Chemical analytical method measuring precipitation weight.
  • Option C (Sedimentation analysis): Only measures settling velocity for silt/clay; cannot be used for gravels and sands.
  • Option D: Gravimetric analysis is not grain size analysis.

Q101: Folk & Ward (1957) Inclusive Graphic Kurtosis Formula

Exam: Geology Paper-II (2021)  |  Authoritative Reference: Sam Boggs Jr. (Principles of Sedimentology and Stratigraphy, Ch. 3, Table 3.3)

Part I: Theoretical Foundation & Concept Masterclass

1. Question & Mathematical Formulation

Question 101: Formulae and verbal scales for graphic size parameters are provided by Folk and Ward (1957). As per the relation, inclusive graphic kurtosis is calculated by which formula ?

  • (A) $K_G = (\phi_{95} - \phi_5) / [2.44 (\phi_{75} - \phi_{25})]$
  • (B) $K_G = (\phi_{95} - \phi_5) / [2.44 (\phi_{75} - \phi_{95})]$
  • (C) $K_G = (\phi_{95} - \phi_5) / [1.44 (\phi_5 - \phi_{25})]$
  • (D) Both (A) and (B) are correct

Correct Answer: (A) $K_G = (\phi_{95} - \phi_5) / [2.44 (\phi_{75} - \phi_{25})]$

Part II: Official Question & Critical Option Dissection

Q101. Formulae and verbal scales for graphic size parameters are provided by Folk and Ward (1957). As per the relation, inclusive graphic kurtosis is calculated by which formula ?
(A) KG = (phi95 - phi5) / [2.44 (phi75 - phi25)]
(B) KG = (phi95 - phi5) / [2.44 (phi75 - phi95)]
(C) KG = (phi95 - phi5) / [1.44 (phi5 - phi25)]
(D) Both (A) and (B) are correct

2. Detailed Geological Masterclass: Folk & Ward Graphic Size Parameters

Robert L. Folk and William C. Ward (1957) revolutionized statistical sedimentology by establishing graphical percentile equations to quantify the grain size frequency distribution of clastic sediments based on cumulative curves plotted in phi units ($\phi = -\log_2 d$):

  • Graphic Kurtosis ($K_G$): Kurtosis measures the ratio between the sorting in the "tails" of the distribution and the sorting in the "central portion". Folk & Ward defined Graphic Kurtosis ($K_G$) as: $$K_G = \frac{\phi_{95} - \phi_5}{2.44 (\phi_{75} - \phi_{25})}$$ where:
    • $(\phi_{95} - \phi_5)$ represents the spread between the 5th and 95th percentiles (the tails).
    • $(\phi_{75} - \phi_{25})$ represents the interquartile range (the central 50%).
    • The factor $2.44$ normalizes a perfect Gaussian curve such that $K_G = 1.00$ (Mesokurtic).
  • Kurtosis Verbal Classification Scale:
    • $K_G < 0.67$: Very Platykurtic (flat-peaked; bimodal tails)
    • $0.67 - 0.90$: Platykurtic
    • $0.90 - 1.11$: Mesokurtic (normal Gaussian distribution)
    • $1.11 - 1.50$: Leptokurtic (excessively peaked)
    • $1.50 - 3.00$: Very Leptokurtic
    • $K_G > 3.00$: Extremely Leptokurtic

Part III: Synthesis Reference Tables & High-Yield Practice

3. Critical Option Elimination & Exam Traps

  • Option A is correct: Exactly matches the standardized Folk and Ward (1957) equation: $K_G = \frac{\phi_{95} - \phi_5}{2.44 (\phi_{75} - \phi_{25})}$.
  • Option B: Denominator contains invalid percentile difference $(\phi_{75} - \phi_{95})$.
  • Option C: Erroneous normalization factor ($1.44$) and incorrect percentile subtraction $(\phi_5 - \phi_{25})$.
  • Option D: Distractor; only formula (A) is mathematically valid.

Q102: Sandstone Classification - Quartz Arenite, Arkose, and Litharenite

Exam: Geology Paper-II (2021)  |  Authoritative Reference: Sam Boggs Jr. (Principles of Sedimentology and Stratigraphy, Ch. 5, p. 145)

Part I: Theoretical Foundation & Concept Masterclass

1. Question & Core Framework Identification

Question 102: Sandstone is categorized into three main types based on their variation in composition and cementing material, they include :
• Quartz Sandstone
• ____________
• Litharenite or lithic sandstone

  • (A) Arkose
  • (B) Greywacke
  • (C) Molasse
  • (D) None of these

Correct Answer: (A) Arkose

Part II: Official Question & Critical Option Dissection

Q102. Sandstone is categorized into three main types based on their variation in composition and cementing material, they include : • Quartz Sandstone, • ___________, • Litharenite or lithic sandstone.
(A) Arkose
(B) Greywacke
(C) Molasse
(D) None of these

2. Detailed Geological Masterclass: The Q-F-L Sandstone Ternary

In the standard classification schemes of Pettijohn (1975) and Folk (1980), terrigenous sandstones with $<15\%$ matrix (arenites) are classified on a triangular diagram whose poles represent the three essential detrital framework components:

Sandstone Family Framework Composition Tectonic & Climatic Significance
1. Quartz Sandstone (Quartz arenite) $\ge 95\%$ Quartz Stable cratonic platform or passive margin; prolonged transport / multi-cycle recycling; supermature.
2. Arkose (Feldspathic arenite) $\ge 25\%$ Feldspar (K-feldspar > Plagioclase) Rapid erosion of uplifted granitic basement / fault blocks in arid or high-relief tectonic settings (immature/submature).
3. Lithic Sandstone (Litharenite) $\ge 25\%$ Unstable rock fragments (clasts) Orogenic foreland basins, trench wedges, or volcanic arcs; rapid deposition close to source.

Greywacke (Wacke): Defined by its high matrix content ($>15\%$ fine detrital silt/clay matrix), representing a separate textural class (wackes vs arenites).
Molasse: A post-orogenic regional stratigraphic facies complex, not a petrographic compositional class.

Part III: Synthesis Reference Tables & High-Yield Practice

3. Critical Option Elimination & Exam Traps

  • Option A (Arkose) is correct: The third cardinal member of the classic compositional arenite trinity (Quartz Arenite, Arkose, Litharenite).
  • Option B (Greywacke): Defined by abundant matrix ($>15\%$ matrix), not an arenite end-member.
  • Option C (Molasse): Stratigraphic basin facies term (foreland basin continental/shallow marine molasse).

Q103: Heavy Mineral Analysis and Sedimentary Provenance

Exam: Geology Paper-II (2021)  |  Authoritative Reference: Sam Boggs Jr. (Principles of Sedimentology and Stratigraphy, Ch. 5, p. 170)

Part I: Theoretical Foundation & Concept Masterclass

1. Question & Analytical Objective

Question 103: The origin of many heavy mineral species is limited to rather specific rock types ; hence, heavies provide information concerning :

  • (A) source rock
  • (B) mineral dispersion pattern
  • (C) quaternary sediments
  • (D) provenance

Correct Answer: (D) provenance

Part II: Official Question & Critical Option Dissection

Q103. The origin of many heavy mineral species is limited to rather specific rock types ; hence, heavies provide information concerning :
(A) source rock
(B) mineral dispersion pattern
(C) quaternary sediments
(D) provenance

2. Detailed Geological Masterclass: Heavy Minerals & Provenance Analysis

Heavy minerals are accessory detrital mineral grains possessing a specific gravity greater than standard bromoform / liquid separation media ($SG > 2.85\text{ g/cm}^3$):

  • Provenance Indicator: Provenance encompasses the complete history of a sedimentary rock, including the source rock lithology, tectonic setting, climate, and paleogeographic location of the parent landmass. Because specific heavy minerals originate in distinctive lithotectonic realms, they serve as the premier tool for provenance reconstruction:
    • Acid Plutonic (Granitic) Source: Monazite, Euhedral Zircon, Tourmaline, Muscovite.
    • Basic / Ultrabasic Igneous Source: Chromite, Ilmenite, Enstatite, Augite, Olivine.
    • Regional Metamorphic Source: Kyanite, Sillimanite, Staurolite, Garnet, Glaucophane.
    • Contact Metamorphic Source: Andalusite, Cordierite, Epidote.
  • Source Rock vs Provenance: While "source rock" (Option A) refers only to the parent lithology, provenance (Option D) is the comprehensive, universally accepted scientific term encompassing source terrain, tectonic setting, transport pathways, and weathering conditions.

Part III: Synthesis Reference Tables & High-Yield Practice

3. Critical Option Elimination & Exam Traps

  • Option D (provenance) is correct: The rigorous, overarching geological term for source area analysis using heavy mineral suites.
  • Option A (source rock): Incomplete subset of provenance; standard academic curricula (Boggs, Pettijohn) designate this study specifically as provenance analysis.
  • Option B & C: Narrow local applications, not the primary scientific objective of heavy mineral petrography.

Q104: Conglomerate Petrography - Rudaceous (Psephitic) Rocks

Exam: Geology Paper-II (2021)  |  Authoritative Reference: Sam Boggs Jr. (Principles of Sedimentology and Stratigraphy, Ch. 5, p. 134)

Part I: Theoretical Foundation & Concept Masterclass

1. Question & Grain-Size Class

Question 104: Conglomerate belongs to which type of sedimentary rocks ?

  • (A) Argillaceous
  • (B) Arenaceous
  • (C) Rudaceous
  • (D) Both (B) and (C) are correct

Correct Answer: (C) Rudaceous

Part II: Official Question & Critical Option Dissection

Q104. Conglomerate belongs to which type of sedimentary rocks ?
(A) Argillaceous
(B) Arenaceous
(C) Rudaceous
(D) Both (B) and (C) are correct

2. Detailed Geological Masterclass: Clastic Grain Size Terminology

Clastic sedimentary rocks are classified based on the dominant diameter of their framework fragments according to the Wentworth size scale:

Grain Size Class Clast Diameter ($d$) Latin / Greek Term Representative Rock Types
Gravel / Boulder / Cobble / Pebble $> 2\text{ mm}$ Rudaceous (Latin: rudus) / Psephitic (Greek: psephos) Conglomerate (rounded clasts), Breccia (angular clasts), Tillite
Sand $0.0625\text{ mm} - 2.0\text{ mm}$ Arenaceous (Latin: arena) / Psammitic (Greek: psammos) Sandstone, Quartz arenite, Arkose, Greywacke
Silt and Clay $< 0.0625\text{ mm}$ Argillaceous (Latin: argilla) / Pelitic (Greek: pelos) Shale, Mudstone, Siltstone, Claystone

Because conglomerate is defined as a clastic rock composed predominantly of rounded gravel-sized fragments ($>2\text{ mm}$), it belongs unequivocally to the rudaceous class.

Part III: Synthesis Reference Tables & High-Yield Practice

3. Critical Option Elimination & Exam Traps

  • Option C (Rudaceous) is correct: Textual definition for gravel-sized rocks ($>2\text{ mm}$) including conglomerates.
  • Option A (Argillaceous): Silt/clay rocks ($<0.0625\text{ mm}$).
  • Option B (Arenaceous): Sand-sized rocks ($0.0625 - 2.0\text{ mm}$).
  • Option D: Conglomerate is strictly rudaceous, never arenaceous.

Q105: Folk (1962) Limestone Classification - Allochems and Intraclasts

Exam: Geology Paper-II (2021)  |  Authoritative Reference: Sam Boggs Jr. (Principles of Sedimentology and Stratigraphy, Ch. 6, p. 186)

Part I: Theoretical Foundation & Concept Masterclass

1. Question & Framework Grain Identification

Question 105: Folk (1962) described the classes of limestone in which framework grains are called allochems which include (i) _________, (ii) oolites, (iii) fossils and (iv) pellets.

  • (A) intraclasts
  • (B) micrite
  • (C) sparry calcite
  • (D) All of these

Correct Answer: (A) intraclasts

Part II: Official Question & Critical Option Dissection

Q105. Folk (1962) described the classes of limestone in which framework grains are called allochems which include (i) _________, (ii) oolites, (iii) fossils and (iv) pellets.
(A) intraclasts
(B) micrite
(C) sparry calcite
(D) All of these

2. Detailed Geological Masterclass: Folk's Carbonate Classification

Robert L. Folk (1959, 1962) classified limestones based on the volumetric proportions of three basic components: (1) Allochems (framework grains), (2) Micrite (microcrystalline carbonate mud matrix, $<4\,\mu\text{m}$), and (3) Sparite (sparry calcite pore-filling cement, $>10\,\mu\text{m}$).

Folk recognized exactly four types of allochems:

  1. Intraclasts: Fragments of penecontemporaneous, semi-consolidated carbonate sediment torn up by wave or storm agitation from within the same depositional basin and redeposited (intrabasinal clasts).
  2. Oolites (Ooids): Spherical, concentrically laminated grains formed by chemical or biological accretion of calcium carbonate around a nucleus in agitated shallow warm waters.
  3. Fossils (Bioclasts): Whole or broken skeletal remains of calcareous organisms (shells, foraminifera, crinoids, algae).
  4. Pellets (Peloids): Structureless, ovoid grains ($0.03 - 0.2\text{ mm}$) composed of microcrystalline calcite, commonly of fecal origin.

Micrite and sparry calcite are interstitial binding media (matrix and cement), NOT allochems!

Part III: Synthesis Reference Tables & High-Yield Practice

3. Critical Option Elimination & Exam Traps

  • Option A (intraclasts) is correct: The fourth cardinal allochem defined by Folk.
  • Option B (micrite): Microcrystalline matrix, strictly distinct from allochems.
  • Option C (sparry calcite): Secondary cement, not an allochem.
  • Option D (All of these): A fatal trap for candidates who confuse carbonate matrix/cement with framework grains.

Q106: Migmatite Genesis and High-Grade Metamorphic Anatexis

Exam: Geology Paper-II (2021)  |  Authoritative Reference: J.D. Winter (Principles of Igneous and Metamorphic Petrology, Ch. 21, p. 411)

Part I: Theoretical Foundation & Concept Masterclass

1. Question & Metamorphic Grade Boundary

Question 106: Migmatite consists of two or more constituents often layered repetitively forming a composite rock found in which metamorphic grade ?

  • (A) Low to medium grade
  • (B) Low grade
  • (C) Medium and high-grade
  • (D) High grade

Correct Answer: (D) High grade

Part II: Official Question & Critical Option Dissection

Q106. Migmatite consists of two or more constituents often layered repetitively forming a composite rock found in which metamorphic grade ?
(A) Low to medium grade
(B) Low grade
(C) Medium and high-grade
(D) High grade

2. Detailed Geological Masterclass: Migmatites and Anatexis

Migmatite (from Greek migma = mixture; Sederholm, 1907) is a composite mega-structured rock occurring in terranes of regional high-grade metamorphism, typically at the transition zone between high-grade metamorphic rocks and granite plutons:

  • Anatectic Melting: Migmatites form when crustal rocks (metapelites, quartzo-feldspathic gneisses) are subjected to ultra-high temperatures ($T > 650^\circ\text{C} - 800^\circ\text{C}$ at $P > 4 - 8\text{ kbar}$, upper amphibolite to granulite facies), reaching the water-saturated granite solidus curve. At this boundary, partial melting (anatexis) begins.
  • Two-Part Structural Anatomy:
    • Leucosome: The light-colored, granitoid quartz-feldspar fraction crystallized from the partial melt.
    • Melanosome (Restite): The dark-colored, refractory residual layer enriched in mafic minerals (biotite, garnet, cordierite, sillimanite) left behind after melt extraction.
    • Mesosome (Paleosome): Remnant patches of un-melted parental metamorphic host rock.
  • Because partial melting of continental crust requires temperatures of upper amphibolite to granulite facies, migmatites are exclusively confined to high-grade metamorphic environments.

Part III: Synthesis Reference Tables & High-Yield Practice

3. Critical Option Elimination & Exam Traps

  • Option D (High grade) is correct: Anatexis and migmatization only occur at high metamorphic grades ($T > 650^\circ\text{C}$).
  • Option A & B (Low to medium grade): Low/medium grades (greenschist to lower amphibolite) cannot reach the temperatures required to melt quartz and feldspar in the presence of $H_2O$.
  • Option C: Medium-grade rocks (e.g., staurolite zone) remain entirely solid-state without leucosome melt segregations.

Q107: Protolith Identification - Shale as the Parental Rock of Slate

Exam: Geology Paper-II (2021)  |  Authoritative Reference: J.D. Winter (Principles of Igneous and Metamorphic Petrology, Ch. 21, p. 420)

Part I: Theoretical Foundation & Concept Masterclass

1. Question & Protolith Lineage

Question 107: Which will be the parental rock for Slate ?

  • (A) Shale
  • (B) Sandstone
  • (C) Limestone
  • (D) All of these

Correct Answer: (A) Shale

Part II: Official Question & Critical Option Dissection

Q107. Which will be the parental rock for Slate ?
(A) Shale
(B) Sandstone
(C) Limestone
(D) All of these

2. Detailed Geological Masterclass: The Pelitic Metamorphic Progression

Metamorphic rocks are grouped by protolith (parent rock) composition. Pelitic rocks (mudrocks rich in aluminum and clay minerals) undergo a classic progressive sequence of regional metamorphism:

$$\text{Shale / Mudstone (Sedimentary Protolith)} \xrightarrow{\approx 200^\circ-300^\circ\text{C}} \textbf{Slate} \xrightarrow{300^\circ-400^\circ\text{C}} \text{Phyllite} \xrightarrow{400^\circ-550^\circ\text{C}} \text{Schist} \xrightarrow{>600^\circ\text{C}} \text{Gneiss}$$
  • Shale $\rightarrow$ Slate: Under incipient directed pressure and low temperature, clay minerals (illite, smectite) in shale recrystallize into microcrystalline white mica (muscovite/sericite) and chlorite oriented perpendicular to the maximum compressive stress direction, imparting excellent planar slaty cleavage.
  • Other Protoliths:
    • Sandstone $\rightarrow$ Quartzite (non-foliated granoblastic texture).
    • Limestone $\rightarrow$ Marble (recrystallized calcite/dolomite).
    • Basalt $\rightarrow$ Greenschist $\rightarrow$ Amphibolite $\rightarrow$ Eclogite.

Part III: Synthesis Reference Tables & High-Yield Practice

3. Critical Option Elimination & Exam Traps

  • Option A (Shale) is correct: Slate is the low-grade metamorphic equivalent of fine-grained pelitic shale/mudstone.
  • Option B (Sandstone): Forms quartzite.
  • Option C (Limestone): Forms marble.

Q108: Foliation Development - Thermodynamic (Dynamothermal) Metamorphism

Exam: Geology Paper-II (2021)  |  Authoritative Reference: J.D. Winter (Principles of Igneous and Metamorphic Petrology, Ch. 23, p. 455)

Part I: Theoretical Foundation & Concept Masterclass

1. Question & Metamorphic Process

Question 108: Foliation in metamorphic rocks developed due to which metamorphic process ?

  • (A) Thermal
  • (B) Dynamic
  • (C) Thermodynamic
  • (D) All of these

Correct Answer: (C) Thermodynamic

Part II: Official Question & Critical Option Dissection

Q108. Foliation in metamorphic rocks developed due to which metamorphic process ?
(A) Thermal
(B) Dynamic
(C) Thermodynamic
(D) All of these

2. Detailed Geological Masterclass: Genesis of Metamorphic Foliation

Foliation is a pervasive, planar fabric in metamorphic rocks defined by the preferred parallel alignment of platy or elongate mineral grains (e.g., micas, chlorite, amphiboles) or by alternating compositional mineral banding:

  • Thermodynamic (Dynamothermal / Regional) Metamorphism: True penetrative metamorphic foliation requires the coupled action of:
    1. Thermal energy ($T$): Drives chemical reaction, solid-state diffusion, and crystal growth of metamorphic phyllosilicates.
    2. Directed differential stress / Dynamic pressure ($\sigma_1 > \sigma_2 > \sigma_3$): Controls the geometric orientation of newly growing crystal lattices (perpendicular to $\sigma_1$) and drives ductile shearing, mechanical rotation, and pressure-solution cleavage.
    Because both thermal and dynamic agents operate simultaneously, this is termed thermodynamic (or dynamo-thermal) metamorphism.
  • Pure Thermal Metamorphism: In contact aureoles around intrusions, heating occurs under quasi-hydrostatic (non-directed) stress; rocks develop unfoliated granoblastic hornfelsic textures.
  • Pure Dynamic Metamorphism: Occurs in narrow brittle fault zones at shallow depths (cataclasites, fault breccias) with minimal thermal recrystallization.

Part III: Synthesis Reference Tables & High-Yield Practice

3. Critical Option Elimination & Exam Traps

  • Option C (Thermodynamic) is correct: The combined thermal recrystallization and directed stress regime that produces pervasive schistosities and gneissose foliations.
  • Option A (Thermal): Generates non-foliated hornfels.
  • Option B (Dynamic): Tends toward brittle pulverization / cataclasis without sustained metamorphic crystal growth unless elevated temperatures are coupled.

Q109: Barrovian Metamorphic Grades - Garnet-Schist as the Highest Grade

Exam: Geology Paper-II (2021)  |  Authoritative Reference: J.D. Winter (Principles of Igneous and Metamorphic Petrology, Ch. 21, p. 430)

Part I: Theoretical Foundation & Concept Masterclass

1. Question & Metamorphic Zonation

Question 109: Amongst the following which is the highest grade of metamorphic rock ?

  • (A) Talc-schist
  • (B) Garnet-schist
  • (C) Mica-schist
  • (D) Chlorite-schist

Correct Answer: (B) Garnet-schist

Part II: Official Question & Critical Option Dissection

Q109. Amongst the following which is the highest grade of metamorphic rock ?
(A) Talc-schist
(B) Garnet-schist
(C) Mica-schist
(D) Chlorite-schist

2. Detailed Geological Masterclass: The Barrovian Zonal Sequence

George Barrow (1893, 1912) established the classic sequence of metamorphic index minerals in pelitic rocks of the Scottish Highlands under intermediate-pressure regional metamorphism:

Barrovian Zone Diagnostic Metamorphic Mineral Metamorphic Grade & Facies Approximate Temperature ($T$)
1. Chlorite Zone Chlorite + Muscovite + Albite Low Grade (Greenschist facies) $300^\circ - 350^\circ\text{C}$
2. Biotite Zone Biotite + Chlorite + Muscovite Low Grade (Greenschist facies) $350^\circ - 450^\circ\text{C}$
3. Garnet Zone Almandine Garnet + Biotite + Muscovite Medium-to-High Grade (Amphibolite facies) $450^\circ - 550^\circ\text{C}$
4. Staurolite Zone Staurolite + Garnet + Biotite Medium Grade (Amphibolite facies) $550^\circ - 600^\circ\text{C}$
5. Kyanite Zone Kyanite + Garnet + Biotite High Grade (Amphibolite facies) $600^\circ - 650^\circ\text{C}$
6. Sillimanite Zone Sillimanite + K-feldspar / Quartz High Grade (Upper Amphibolite / Granulite) $> 650^\circ\text{C}$

Talc-schist is a hydrated ultrabasic metamorphic rock of the greenschist facies ($300-400^\circ\text{C}$). Chlorite-schist marks the lowest greenschist grade ($300^\circ\text{C}$). General mica-schist spans greenschist to lower amphibolite. Therefore, Garnet-schist represents the highest metamorphic grade among the listed choices.

Part III: Synthesis Reference Tables & High-Yield Practice

3. Critical Option Elimination & Exam Traps

  • Option B (Garnet-schist) is correct: The appearance of almandine garnet marks the transition into the amphibolite facies ($T \approx 450-550^\circ\text{C}$), the highest grade in the list.
  • Option D (Chlorite-schist): Low-grade greenschist facies ($300^\circ\text{C}$).
  • Option A (Talc-schist): Low-grade greenschist alteration of ultramafic protoliths.
  • Option C (Mica-schist): Broad category; when unqualified, it precedes or encompasses the biotite zone prior to garnet entry.
